papers.title: Between the Lines: Multi-turn Contextual Investment Advice Detection
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly power financial conversational assistants, detecting investment advice in natural language has become a critical regulatory and safety challenge. Unlike explicit single-turn recommendations, investment advice often emerges implicitly and progressively over multi-turn conversations, shaped by user intent, delivery style, and contextual buildup. We introduce the first comprehensive framework for detecting both sequential and contextual investment advice in dialogue settings. Central to our approach is a modular, top-down synthetic data generation pipeline that systematically spans a taxonomy of advisory trajectories using an axis-bucket-descriptor schema. We simulate both benign and high-risk conversations across diverse user personas, financial instruments, and risk tiers, and evaluate detection capabilities using LLM-as-a-Judge with entropy-based uncertainty diagnostics. Our results show that contextual advisory detection remains substantially more challenging than sequential cases, even under few-shot prompting with tailored demonstrations. This work lays the foundation for scalable guardrail development in high-stakes, compliance-sensitive domains, where advisory risk is often subtle, distributed, and perception-dependent.

papers.title: NoLBERT-Calls: Reading Earnings Calls Without Hindsight
papers.abstract: Language models are now a standard tool for measuring what managers say on earnings calls, but the encoders behind these measures were usually pretrained on text from the same years a backtest covers. Holding out a test period does not remove that hindsight, because it sits in the features. We adapt NoLBERT, an encoder pretrained only on text published between 1976 and 1995, to earnings calls without letting it read anything dated after 31 December 2023. The calls supply the training signal themselves: every analyst question is followed by management's answer, and the model learns to pick that answer out from the other answers of the same call. We test on every US call from January 2025 to October 2026 (20,323 calls, 254,575 questions) and make every modeling choice on calls from 2024. The adapted model, NoLBERT-Calls-2023, ranks the true answer first for 78.0% of questions (95% interval 77.8-78.2; chance 8.0%), against 26.3% before adaptation. It is 1.0 point ahead of a call-adapted ChronoBERT, 3.4 points ahead of a call-adapted FinBERT, and 18.7 and 19.8 points ahead of the best off-the-shelf retriever and BM25. A year-by-year test over 2013-2026 finds no look-ahead premium: relative to a model adapted only through 2012, the released model does no better on the years it was trained on than on years it never saw. The price of the cutoff is compute: under one shared 150-minute recipe NoLBERT adapts least well of four encoders, and its lead comes from a longer, staged adaptation of about 13 GPU-hours.

papers.title: Corporate Stances on Societal Issues in the US
papers.abstract: When do firms take public positions on divisive societal issues and why? We assemble a comprehensive dataset on corporate stance-taking in the United States, using large language models to read 52,000 news articles and press releases about 836 companies that belonged to the S&P 500 at any point between 2008 and 2025. We identify 9,917 stances on nine partisan issues such as climate change, abortion, and racial discrimination. We show that stance-taking increased fourfold after 2008 and peaked in 2021. It is overwhelmingly liberal and concentrated among the largest firms. A quarter of stances give no explicit business justification. Stance-taking is only weakly related to lobbying and campaign contributions and, unlike them, does not follow the electoral cycle. Instead, firms tend to speak when media coverage and public interest in an issue peak. Together, these findings suggest that stance-taking can be understood as a contribution to broad policy debates rather than a strategy to shape policies that affect firms' core business. Finally, we investigate whose views corporate stances represent. Consumer-facing firms take more stances, and firms whose consumers lean Democratic take more liberal stances on issues other than climate. Companies with larger shares of Democratic employees, executives, and board members also take more liberal stances. Exploiting within-firm variation, we find that having more Democrats among a company's leadership increases liberal stance-taking, while having more women increases stance-taking on gender-related issues and abortion.

papers.title: Short Windows, Unmodelled Costs, Unknown Cutoffs: A Pre-Registered Evidence Audit of 91 LLM Trading Papers
papers.abstract: Papers on large-language-model (LLM) trading agents and alpha mining report Sharpe ratios that would be remarkable in any other part of empirical finance. We audit the evidence behind those numbers. Before coding a single paper we pre-registered a population of 91 papers from a curated corpus of LLM trading research, a ten-field coding rubric, an analysis script and five directional hypotheses, and committed all of them to version control. Every code is backed by a verbatim quote that a script checks against the paper's text, and a second, blind coder recoded a random 20%. Of the 75 papers with a trading test, 51% deduct no trading costs and only 9% model costs from data; the median test window is 12 months, and a quarter of windows are six months or shorter. Among the 51 papers whose test window is not known to lie after the model's training cutoff, 98% neither test after the cutoff, nor evaluate live, nor use a chronologically consistent model. Only 9% report a multiplicity-adjusted result, and just five papers combine deducted costs, a leakage control and a reported trial count. Two of the five hypotheses pass (short windows; uncontrolled look-ahead). Three fail: more papers report a trial count than we predicted, though most of those counts are repeated random seeds rather than the number of strategies searched; and the predicted links between headline Sharpe and test-window length, and between headline Sharpe and costs, are not detectable in the 13 papers that state a headline Sharpe in their abstract or conclusion. We release the codes, quotes and script, and propose a six-line reporting minimum.

papers.title: CFOs Meet LLMs
papers.abstract: Business sentiment is closely watched, but measurement is slow and costly: surveys reach a limited number of firms, arrive periodically, and take time to field and compile. We show that large language models hold the potential to address some of these shortcomings. We prompt an LLM to role-play as the CFO of a specific company on a specific date, for every public-company CFO who responded to the Duke--Federal Reserve CFO Survey from 2002- 2025. We find that LLM-generated forecasts reasonably match the cross-section of CFO expectations, with accuracy increasing with the amount of information provided to the LLM.
